EAVD scientists utilize a variety of imaging and spectral data formats, which pose challenges when trying to integrate and compare datasets. To facilitate visualization and comprehension, we are providing an web-based tool that allows for the graphical display of spectral data, including phase information, on a EAVD lab website. This tool, now in its enhanced version, features an improved user interface, bug fixes, and the capability to show multiple spectra in a comparative table, accessible through the URL http://eavd.lanl.gov/tools/ (Figure 1, right).

The Southern Atlantic Ocean's formation began through a process where the African and South American plates moved apart, initially centered under the Guinea Highlands and the Brazilian Shield. This process later shifted to the Central Atlantic Oceanic Fracture Zone. The ages of the sea floor created at this ridge system are not uniform, with some parts forming up to 100 million years earlier than others. To better understand this, researchers used advanced techniques to analyze the geometry of this fracture zone and its surrounding areas, as well as the speed and direction of the plates, based on land-based data and the position of the South American plate from ancient magnetic field patterns. They also compared this to a specific model of the Atlantic's evolution. Their findings suggest that a significant tear in the lithosphere under the South Atlantic may have been caused by upwelling mantle material around 120 million years ago. This is further supported by the discovery of the Rio Grande Rise in the Southern Atlantic and the Rio Grande Rift on the Brazilian Shield. The upwelling material also explains the complex structure of the Central Atlantic Fracture Zone, characterized by numerous mini-spreading centers. The history of this zone can be divided into three main phases. The first phase, from 129 to 110 million years ago, is linked to the Rio Grande Rise-Rio Grande Rift system and the South Atlantic fissure zone. The second phase, from 96 to 84 million years ago, is associated with

Undefined target regions in medical segmentation are challenging to annotate accurately, which can be addressed by incorporating boundary-sensitive information, typically abundant in region-based annotations. This information is underutilized in medical image segmentation due to the high cost of boundary propagation. Recent advancements in self-supervised learning allow models to extract implicit background information from unlabeled data and transfer it to the target domain. However, further studies have shown that these models overestimate the target region. A novel framework, Boundary-sensitive Information Optimization (BIO), is proposed to efficiently balance difficult target regions and excessive pseudo labels using abundant difficult negative samples and compact high-quality labels within the model. The proposed model integrates difficult target information, useful pseudo labels and boundary-sensitive information to achieve effective detection and segmentation of the target region. Furthermore, BIO applies difficult negative sample mining to expand difficult negative samples in easy self-supervised labels, and introduces a path-consistency loss to generate boundary-sensitive information from undefined pseudo labels in target regions. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that BIO achieves superior performance compared to state-of-theart methods.

Video games have long been a rich source of assistance for humans in understanding and addressing real-world challenges. This study explores the potential of VR-based gaming experiences with complex, socially realistic applications to improve problem-solving for real-world problems. Specifically, we investigate how interacting with a virtual agent that leads a well-known social simulation, 'Dungeons and Dragons,' can convey beneficial knowledge to a player when applied to a simple decision-making task. In this experiment, we manipulate the leading agent's thoughts and intentions, as well as its communication style, to examine the effects on the player's learning and generalization abilities. Our findings suggest that the player can learn efficiently from the leading agent's intentions, gaining access to counterfactual information inaccessible when only observing the agent's actions. Conversely, we observe that excessive clarity in intentions may hinder the player's ability to generalize their learning. Furthermore, we explore the role of mentalizing, or understanding the agent's perspective of another, in influencing how effectively a player can apply their learning. Our results contribute to our comprehension of the theoretical underpinnings of human learning from social leaders and the potential of VR-based learning from complex agents for tackling real-world leadership and management challenges.

Traditionally, word embeddings are evaluated based on their current accuracy in performing Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), yet there's a growing concern that evaluating them for predicting semantic change over time might have more significance. This paper aims to introduce a method for identifying and evaluating semantic shifts through a systematic evaluation of the ability to detect Concept-Associated Words (CAWs) that experienced a shift in meaning across various domains. The proposed framework is designed to automatically detect semantic shifts by using words whose associations with concepts have changed over a specific time period. Moreover, it can be adapted to manually select senses and evaluate the detected semantic shifts by comparing the results with a standard metric, sense distribution F1-score. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the proposed framework was applied to English Wikipedia, automatically identifying 50 prominent semantic shifts, including the decline of the 'paper' concept and the rise of the 'digital' concept in 20 years from 2001 to 2011.

We propose a novel set of functions within the parton landscape, categorized as $k_\perp$-dependent parton distribution functions (pDFs) and pseudo parton distribution functions (ppDFs), which incorporate transverse momentum and longitudinal momentum fractions while excluding the hadron's longitudinal momentum direction. Although the set of functions available for analysis in a hadron is constrained, we believe the pDFs and pDFs, which exist independently, offer greater flexibility. If accessible experimentally, these functions would provide invaluable insights into the complex structure of hadrons. We outline the theoretical underpinnings of pDFs and pDFs, focusing on global fit analysis, and discuss the relationships between these sets of functions, the three-dimensional structure of hadrons, and relevant physical processes. Finally, we describe the connections between pDFs/pDFs and traditional PDFs/kTFPs, as well as the influence of gauge links in these functions.

The intricate folding and knotting of proteins are complex biological phenomena, and understanding the underlying mechanisms is hindered by limited experimental and theoretical insights. Researchers are actively exploring the relationship between a protein's three-dimensional structure and its folding and knotting processes. A key area of investigation involves identifying the biological significance of certain topological features, such as the arrangement of backbone loops, and how they influence the protein's overall structure. In this study, a novel method is developed to extract stable loop arrangements from protein structures, and this method is employed to find similar configurations in multiple protein instances, notably in a bacteriophage protein with a knot that opens under force. By analyzing the identified loop arrangements, force-extension data, and molecular dynamics simulations, it is demonstrated that specific configurations contribute to bending pathways of the protein backbone, leading to the formation of the knot during the opening process.

To address the mystery behind the cosmic coincidence problem, early dark energy models were proposed with a plan to resolve the issue by making the influence of dark energy on the universe's history more symmetric. Based on this principle, a new class of Hubble parameter models was created that incorporates both early and late periods of dark energy's impact. Using a specific early slow-roll model and analyzing the 2018 Planck and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) data, researchers identified a 95% confidence limit for the early influence of dark energy. They found that these models fit the data well when restricted to a certain percentage of the critical density of the universe. This limitation is quite stringent and has significant implications for the overall development and evolution of the universe's history. Furthermore, the researchers highlighted the necessity for future large-scale structure surveys to obtain even tighter constraints on these types of Hubble parameter models.

We define two new subgroups, symplectic mapping classes and homotopy classes, within the symplectic mapping group of a blowup of a closed symplectic manifold. By extending results from Birman and Hilden for surfaces, we prove that for a fixed symplectic form, the corresponding symplectic mapping type groups are equivalent. Moreover, the group of symplectic mapping classes is shown to be the fundamental covering of the symplectic mapping type group of homotopy classes. These concepts can be utilized to investigate the homotopy structure of the symplectic mapping group. Moreover, the relationship between the various homotopy sequences can be employed to derive the homotopy sequences of the relevant groups.

A rigorous mathematical framework has been established to derive a unified, absolutely continuous spectrum representation for a broad spectrum of relativistic and nonrelativistic, rotationally symmetric quantum field theories. This representation provides the foundation for a detailed analysis of the representation structure of the Wigner group within both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum theories. Based on this analysis, sufficient conditions have been set to determine when a mass gap exists or, alternatively, when the vacuum pole in the 2-particle scattering amplitude implies Nambu-Goldstone modes arising from spontaneous breaking of Poincare or Galilean symmetries. The resulting Soffer-Tomasiq Theorem has been proven to hold for both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories with interaction terms that may vary, including polynomial and Coulomb potentials. The derivation of this theorem constitutes the first instance of a rigorous, unified result applicable to both types of quantum field theories with sufficiently broad conditions.

Current methods for generating synthetic data through rule-based or human-defined operations are highly costly, inflexible, and impractical for complex tasks, particularly when dealing with diverse patterns of difficulty. Although counterfactuals have been previously used to test models' biases and prejudices, no systematic approach exists for creating phrasal counterfactuals that account for context and complexity. To address this gap, we introduce DISCO, a context-sensitive framework that utilizes a large language model to create phrasal counterfactuals across multiple domains, including demographics, psychology, and sociology. By generating a wide range of difficult cases automatically, our approach extends existing evaluations and creates benchmarks that challenge models to differentiate between subtle distinctions. We observe that models struggle with these phrasal counterfactuals and perform poorly on them compared to simpler, easier counterfactuals.

The total coloring of a graph involves assigning colors to both edges and vertices such that no adjacent or identical elements share the same color. Among various types of constraints, sum distinguishing total colorings (SDTC) are particularly relevant, requiring the colored neighborhoods of any non-adjacent vertices to differ in color composition. This paper delves into examining the minimum colors needed for certain classes of circulant graphs to meet the SDTC condition. For some graphs, we establish the minimum color requirement, while for others, we identify specific conditions under which this need can be met. The analysis covers a range of circulant graphs, including those with up to four distinct lengths.

Researchers have successfully grown high-quality Heusler films using remote epitaxy on the surface of graphene that sits atop an aluminum oxide substrate as a reference. By fine-tuning how these films form, scientists can optimize their quality through a substrate's surface features and resistance to atomic diffusion. Research has particularly focused on the complex process of growing the chalcopyrite structure of materials like $Cu_2MnSnS_4$ and $Cu_2OsSnS_4$ due to its mismatch with the underlying graphene lattice. Heusler films were also evaluated using various techniques, with a key finding that their performance is linked to the thickness of a specific layer within the graphene structure. Notably, increasing this layer's thickness led to a significant improvement in optical properties, indicating the potential for better film stability and reduced defects.

A code is considered $ \Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear if it derives from a ring code via the $\Z_{p^2}$-$\Z_p$ mapping and is equivalent to a code in the multivariate ring $\Z_{p^2}^{\Z_p^{2n}}$ for any size $ 2n $. Code equivalence in $\Z_{p^2}^{ \Z_p^{2n}}$ to $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear codes has been investigated in terms of its associated parameters and code classes, and we prove that such codes possess a null space that retains the $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linearity property and a dimension formula that accounts for code equivalence and depends solely on code weight and length. Codes and their duals are proven to share length and weight characteristics, and codes with maximum code parameter ratio are shown to be potentially good multi-error-correcting codes with a large code parameter ratio, and an example of a high-ratio code is analyzed in detail.

The effectiveness of various polymer injection techniques, such as those used in oil recovery and contaminant blocking, relies on the formation of an elongated structure known as a "plug." This phenomenon is attributed to the higher viscosity of polymers in comparison to water. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanism of plug creation is still not fully comprehended. It is hypothesized that regions of polymer concentration begin to accumulate near the channel walls due to the onset of a first-order velocity gradient, and eventually merge into a plug when the injected polymer amount is sufficient. In order to test this theory, a simplified model consisting of two channel components was used, and numerical simulations were conducted to examine the injection profiles of polymer plugs. The simulations indicated that injecting a polymer solution into a water-filled channel results in a characteristic coiled shape, and this feature is less pronounced in channels filled with a more viscous fluid. Furthermore, the study found that the position of the plug's tail is influenced by the fluid's viscosities and the injection rate, and this can be better understood by considering the balance between the convective and diffusive forces at play.

A significant portion of public datasets is tagged with a single label per instance, 
however, many such datasets actually contain a wealth of underexplored, multi-labeled opportunities. 
In this study, we investigate the potential for identifying multi-labeled instances within datasets that are currently single-labeled. 
Building upon existing techniques for multi-label classification that rely on label correlations, we develop Extract-MLB, a method to extract multi-labeled instances from single-labeled data without requiring manual annotation. 
This method utilizes the label connections to expand each dataset's scope by having each dataset member's unlabeled, highly-labeled neighbors to be identified. 
Our approach has been tested on three distinct public datasets, each with a specific task type: image classification, pseudo-labeled data for 3D object detection from 2D images, and self-supervised training. 
The results show that our method significantly boosts performance when compared to baseline methods. 
Additionally, we have made the expanded datasets available to the research community via an online repository.

For a wide range of materials, such as those exhibiting memory effects and irreversible processes, complex time behavior can be modeled by using fractional time derivatives within the phase-field equation. This research extends the concept of energy dissipation, originally proposed by Becker and Elder, to include fractional time derivatives, by defining a new functional that analogously represents the dissipation of energy. A similar structure to this new energy dissipation principle is verified, with the rate of energy change equating to the sum of dissipation and work done, all within a rigorous mathematical framework. A key requirement for this verification is the application of a modified inequality, recently introduced, to overcome the limitations arising from the nonlinearity of the fractional time derivative. A similar result to the classical case of 2nd kind inequality is derived for the local noninteger time derivative model. A similar result to this new energy dissipation principle for the nonlocal Caputo derivative is verified under the assumption of localizing the fractional time derivative. A key requirement for this equality is the establishment of a corresponding analog to the pointwise uniqueness property. A crucial aspect of this research is the derivation of a bound on the density of the probability measure associated with the solution, with this bound being of the form $\rho\leq C\exp\left(\int_0^t k(s)\ds\right)$, with this bound being a crucial component in proving the energy dissipation principle. The Gesztesy-Hochrainer-Haase construction for separating bound states from continuous states in self-adjoint extensions of symmetric operators forms a categorical pattern. This construction can be represented as a category of adjoint pairs, and the category of symmetric operators with their continuous self-adjoint extensions is a full subcategory of this structure, preserving the adjoint relationships. This equivalence holds for a specific idempotent ID^op -> ID functor, and the relevant idempotent splits within this subcategory.

We propose a new theory to explain the cause of high-energy gamma-rays found in nearby slow, energetic radio galaxies. Observations show that these galaxies emit no significant gamma-rays, with energy levels below 10^11 electron volts. Our hypothesis involves a magnetic field around the accretion disks of their active galactic cores, which traps energetic particles and prevents gamma-ray emission. A condition has been established to meet this condition, which, in most active galaxies, results in weak or absent gamma-rays. The condition is met by quasistellar active galaxies but not by active quasars, which could account for the observed high-energy gamma-ray differences between these two types of objects around the active centers of galaxies. The condition for this hypothesis to hold is that high-energy gamma-ray flux would remain less than the observed upper limits when considering nearby radio galaxies, demonstrating its validity. Additionally, this theory can be tested by observing high-energy gamma-rays from galaxies with colliding jets.

This research reexamines the critical but underappreciated choice of portfolio allocation strategies, moving away from restrictive assumptions of pre-set positions or pre-set returns. We develop and apply a flexible two-step methodology that simultaneously addresses the portfolio allocation and the position/return distribution questions. Our Markov-switching model, focusing solely on return data, identifies the optimal allocation strategies that maximize the desired performance metrics. Notable achievements of this approach include the 16% improvement in average monthly returns compared to a 60/40 benchmark using our RFS-Opt model, the 25% reduction in monthly return volatility with our DSA-Opt model, and the alignment of risk-adjusted returns with the risk-free rate for various benchmarks using the RFS-Opt strategy.

Various techniques have been developed for S1 and S2 heart sound classification, but most struggle with correct identification due to noise and individual differences affecting waveform distortion. To address this challenge, a new convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture was proposed which leverages the power of deep learning to handle these distortions. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed CNN achieves the best performance among all tested CNN models and significantly outperforms the leading non-neural network method, including support vector machine (SVM), particularly in cases with noisy data. Notably, when no noise is present, the proposed CNN still delivers a 15% improvement in accuracy compared to the leading non-neural method.

The emergence of wearable technology has significantly accelerated the development of medical care, with modern devices capable of monitoring vital signs and providing real-time data to both patients and medical professionals. Furthermore, the introduction of machine learning techniques has enabled the creation of compact algorithms run on these devices, delivering real-time predictions and seamless integration with existing systems. However, significant challenges persist, primarily centered on data privacy concerns and limited storage capabilities of wearable devices. In response, this paper presents the FedHealth transfer learning framework, which leverages the potential of federated learning to train models on local data without external transmission, thus safeguarding patient information and minimizing the data requirements on wearable devices. The FedHealth framework combines a federated attention unlearning module and a local prediction module to transfer knowledge from a teacher model to a smaller student model on the wearable device, enabling real-time patient data analysis and medical diagnosis. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superior performance of FedHealth in terms of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency when compared to existing methods.

Portfolio optimization is crucial in the finance sector and has been extensively studied over the years. It involves determining the best allocation of investment funds to maximize returns while minimizing risks. This review paper delves into advanced moment-based portfolio optimization methods by examining how higher-order moments impact portfolio performance and risk management. The study summarizes existing research using practical examples and discusses the limitations of linear programming in solving complex optimization problems with multiple objectives.

The coincidence dilemma suggests a striking discrepancy between the predicted and observed dark matter distribution within the Milky Way's dark matter disk. This discrepancy arises due to the smooth simulation-predicted dark matter profile in contrast to the point-like observed data. Our research proposes that the dark matter density within this disk may be significantly lower than currently estimated, thereby resolving this dilemma. A novel two-fluid simulation model featuring dark matter and baryons as viscoelastic fluids with self-regulating properties is presented. The model's implementation in a Milky Way-like galaxy results in a significantly reduced dark matter density within the disk. The Model's predictions are also validated through observational data and the control of the 'rotation curve crisis' and the dark matter disk's size are confirmed.

This paper presents a unique approach to accelerating software testing and debugging,
by automatically generating test cases and input data. We identify the essentials for
streamlining these activities within a team environment, and outline several
tools that align with our framework, providing a starting point for further
research in this area. Our observations and conclusions can significantly expedite
the work of our team and similar groups, by offering a structured way to share
tests, inputs, and patches.

In a control problem involving a toggling action and a C\'adl\'ag cost function on a finite time frame, our study aims to prove that the value function is lower semi-continuous, ensuring the existence of an optimal strategy. However, due to the discontinuous nature of the problem, weak convergence is likely required to find a optimal solution, which presents a significant challenge given the set of states is not compact.

If certain leptoquarks exist, their presence could be revealed through their unique signatures, specifically by searching for scenarios where they appear in pairs but with different masses. An initiated study outlines a strategy to identify these unequal leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider. This strategy involves analyzing decay patterns that result in final states with two top quarks, one lepton, and additional missing transverse energy, which can be produced through various processes such as electroweak and strong interactions. The study also considers the impact of initial parton interactions and demonstrates the effectiveness of using machine learning techniques, specifically using linearly separable decision boundaries, to distinguish between the pair production and single leptoquark processes. The findings suggest that this approach could allow for the discovery of heavy gauge leptoquks with a mass of 2.5 TeBs, while also providing a more in-depth analysis of the various involved processes.

As deep learning techniques advance, they have started to surpass human performance on various benchmarks across different fields of biology and chemistry. Given the potential for these achievements, there is a growing demand to create more effective methods of training researchers using automated systems for sequence analysis. Due to the high dimensionality and complexity of sequence data, as well as the lack of explicit labels that define the relationship between input sequences and target sequences, developing effective learning algorithms has proven to be a challenging task. In order to enhance the effectiveness of deep learning models for sequence learning, researchers have developed the Guided Learning of Temporal Sequences (GLTS) algorithm, which explicitly models the temporal dependencies between consecutive sequences. By leveraging this information, the model achieves superior performance on datasets from the fields of biology and chemistry and has also been applied to the creation of effective methods of training researchers using automated systems. The code for these systems is available on the corresponding source code repository.

Photodissociation regions (PDRs) at the interface between a galaxy's warm ionized and cold molecular gases are known to be the primary source of neutral carbon line emission. However, there is debate regarding whether these lines also originate from the molecular gas reservoir itself, where the temperature of the neutral gas is significantly lower. In this paper, we investigate the presence and properties of warm carbon in the same temperature range as the PDR component, and identify a distinct population of subthermally excited Ci atoms that exist within the molecular gas reservoir. This population of subthermally excited Ci atoms is found to be linearly correlated with the PDR component, and shows that this population is determined by the hydrogen molecule flux and the gas density surrounding the hydrogen molecule reservoir. As a result, the subthermally excited Ci population may provide important constraints on PDR theory. Furthermore, it is also found that this distinct population of subthermally excited Ci atoms can be used as a new and independent probe of the hydrogen molecule flux in local galaxies, in agreement with PDR theory predictions.

To address the persistent discrepancies in the dilepton and diphoton branching fractions along with the lepton universality issues at LHCb, we propose a vector-like nature for the Standard Model in a specific energy domain, where quarks and gluons exhibit composite characteristics mediated by a new force at the Poyle scale, $\Lambda$. Through the analysis of relevant experimental data in both $B$ and $pp$ colliders, the vector-like model is thoroughly constrained, allowing us to extract a $\Lambda$ scale of $24.4~\text{GeV}$, thereby simultaneously resolving the inconsistencies in dilepton, diphoton, and universality issues while contradicting LHC measurements.

Given positive integers $d$ and $w$, we determine conditions under which a arrangement exists consisting of binary vectors of length $d$, where any two vectors are separated by a Hamming distance of at least $2w$. The goal is to find the maximum size, $\mathcal{A}(d, 2w)$, of such an arrangement. If the distance constraint can be met by rotating any vector $d$ times, we can reconstruct the arrangement in any base up to 10 by matching the binary representation with a numeric sequence. We identify specific conditions where this is possible for two-weight constraints. Additionally, we examine arrangements where the Hamming distance between any two vectors is exactly $2w$, determining conditions where an algebraic structure can be formed. Finally, we relate this exact distance property to a graph theory concept, finding that such an arrangement corresponds to a circle graph if the distance is $2w-1$.

This paper presents a novel approach to musical instrument classification, adapting a hierarchical structure to enhance classification accuracy. By dividing the task into two subcategories, we first classify music based on a binary categorization and then apply a specialized, 50-class HINet model to identify specific instruments. This strategic decomposition of the problem yields a significant improvement in accuracy, achieving a 5% increase over the baseline musical instrument recognition model.

To facilitate the development of NLP models capable of resolving complex, fact-based questions using textual documents, existing datasets are frequently employed. Focusing on the scientific domain, we present an expansive dataset comprised of 37,000 paired questions and answers derived from research articles. These pairs are extracted from the underlying content of the documents and represent advanced, information-seeking questions that demand comprehensive responses. Additionally, we outline the NLP capabilities necessary to tackle such sophisticated problems.

We've developed highly precise simulations of pulsar timing array signals generated by inspiraling binary stars with elliptical orbits, corresponding to over 2000 post-Newtonian moments and representing the effects of multiple gravitational wave waveforms. These simulations are applicable to a wide range of binaries and account for various factors such as binary orientation, radial velocity, and the potential impact on nearby pulsars. However, such high precision comes with a significant computational cost. We analyzed the precision-to-computation time trade-off for different scenarios and determined the appropriate level of precision for each, based on the expected number of detected signals.

We study the TASEP velocity process, a velocity-based re-writing of the total asymmetric exclusion process. Analysis of TASEP reveals it can be simplified to velocity-based particle interactions, allowing for a corresponding totalistic version. We establish that the standard ASEP is equivalent to the totalistic ASEP velocity process, extending this equivalence to cyclic variants of the process.

As the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic continues to spread, governments and health services worldwide are taking measures to slow its progression. This situation highlights the global impact of the disease and the need for robust mathematical models to predict the effects of these interventions. Multiple mathematical models have been developed to analyze this situation, and in doing so, they aim to provide a basis upon which hypotheses regarding the epidemic's behavior can be tested. Here, we examine the various mathematical frameworks that have been utilized in this context and explore their potential applications to the ongoing pandemic. Furthermore, we investigate the underlying transmission dynamics models that underpin these mathematical frameworks.

This study examines the unique properties of a Majorana fermion model, which is 
mathematically equivalent to a free fermion system. Despite this, it exhibits 
characteristics of a random matrix model, specifically predicting that the 
Majorana model will display the following: (i) the mean entropy between two 
systems of sizes $N_1$ and $N_2$ will converge to the von Neumann entropy of 
the smaller system divided by the larger system's size in the limit of a large 
system; (ii) entropy fluctuations will decrease as the system size increases, 
exhibiting a $1/\sqrt{N}$ behavior; (iii) level spacing distributions, 
entropies between system states, and number operator distributions will all 
follow Gaussian patterns; and (iv) in the limit of a large system, entropy 
calculations using the mean level spacing will yield the same results as those 
using entropy fluctuations. These findings are verified through numerical 
simulations.

Acronyms are extensively used across diverse domains and take advantage of
character limits in certain platforms such as Twitter. Their popularity stems from being concise and fashionable, yet their ambiguity poses significant challenges in understanding contexts, particularly when combined with preceding characters that denote different meanings. This dual nature makes acronym analysis essential in fields like information extraction, natural language processing, and coreference resolution. In this study, we examine the intricate nature of acronym recognition and resolution, highlighting key characteristics such as the fixed length, lack of spacing, and varying surrounding characters. Our research proposes the MadDog system, an innovative approach utilizing contextual embeddings and ensembling techniques to achieve accurate acronym disambiguation. Contextual embeddings, drawn from models including BERT and BioBERT, capture the contextual information, while ensembling techniques integrate the target text, source acronym, and reverse acronym for a comprehensive analysis. Our web interface provides a user-friendly experience, facilitating the annotation of web-derived data and submission of novel ensembling approaches. Our findings demonstrate the utility of the MadDog system in coreference resolution, contextual sarcasm detection, and sarcasm-enhanced web data annotation, providing a robust framework for further exploration and innovation in acronym-related research.

Converting two spinors into a bosospinor, transforming a bosospinor into a boson, and converting a boson into a fermion, all through atom-molecule transitions, can be achieved by using light-based synthesizers to create various types of artificial atoms and molecules from indium arsenide quantum dots. Despite being a well-established phenomenon in two-body systems, this phenomenon has yet to be fully harnessed in many-body systems due to limitations posed by excited state decays. Through a breakthrough, we have now demonstrated both two-way spinor-bosospinor and bosospinor-boson transformations even in multi-body systems, by carefully selecting synthetic states that are immune to decay processes. Specifically, we have identified two new types of bosonic states that can result in large spinor components and can be directly synthesized from a single spinor atom state. These states offer potential for further study into highly controllable systems with rich internal structures.

Due to its high density, low cost, and reliability, DNA storage has quickly become a leading storage technology for massive data sets. Nevertheless, its primary drawback lies in the difficulty of updating specific pieces of information, which usually necessitates re-synthesizing a large proportion of the storage library. To address this issue, a novel strategy called the hierarchical storage framework was proposed just two years ago, which organizes data into multiple levels of complexity. Although this method increases high-density access efficiency, its ability to handle updates is limited to simple corrections. In this research, we significantly advance this concept by introducing a new scheme that utilizes "bridge" sequences to facilitate more effective information updates within each hierarchy and between levels. Our experiments show that this innovative design enables 99.999999% successful refresh operations between adjacent levels with a relatively low update library size of 0.001%, which is 3 orders of magnitude smaller than the conventional approach requiring 0.1% success rate.

Recently, research has focused on novel topological phases characterized by nodal surfaces, where we examine the concepts underlying these structures through the lens of photonic systems and other analogous setups. By exploring these implementations, we aim to provide a clearer understanding of the fundamental topological invariances associated with nodal surfaces in momentum space.

This project aims to automate the identification, classification, and delineation of brain tumors in MRI images, which is of vital importance for the early detection and diagnosis of intracranial abnormalities. Accurate and timely identification of brain tumors can significantly expedite the process and reduce the workload of neurologists and radiologists. However, interpreting MRI images remains a challenging task due to variations in quality and the subtle differences between healthy brain tissue and tumors. To overcome these difficulties, recent advancements in Deep Learning have led to the development of image analysis techniques that assist radiologists in their diagnostic processes. In this study, we present a novel end-to-end Deep Learning framework called MAG-Net, which is capable of identifying, classifying, and segmenting gliomas in MRI images. Our model employs a graph attention mechanism to identify and connect related lesions, and a multi-task learning approach to simultaneously perform multiple tasks. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that MAG-Net outperforms leading segmentation and classification models, exhibiting robust performance even on images with complex patterns.

This paper presents a novel approach to accurately estimate shadow issues in inverse rendering without producing ghost artifacts, utilizing differentiable rendering frameworks. By modeling light occlusion as a difference between two point light shadows, a single evaluation is shown to be nearly as effective as using two light evaluation calls. Building upon shadow importance estimation techniques from previous research, this paper leverages a bias-reducing network to minimize the gap between training and inference losses. By training the network to minimize this gap rather than directly estimating the shadow importance, the need for issue regression networks is circumvented. The proposed method is integrated with MipNeRF360, with results demonstrating a 20% improvement in accuracy over the baseline, with limited computational cost. The code is publicly available for review.

A cutting-edge deep learning approach to deinterlacing has been introduced, utilizing minute amounts of training data, including just 10 minutes of cardiology video. In contrast to conventional methods that depend on analyzing entire frames, our method focuses on processing individual fields and leverages information from neighboring fields within the same scanline. Due to its ability to handle input at a field level, our model excels in tasks such as tracking moving objects, even when there are significant movements between fields. Experimental evaluations demonstrate superior performance of our method against multiple deep learning baselines and state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks. Further, our method achieves remarkable results in real-time applications, particularly in cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, surpassing current standards with only 2x computational cost.

Our analysis of the neutron distribution in atomic nuclei was conducted using the Dirac-Bruckner method and our findings were compared to the results from non-relativistic mean field theory. In a study of 28 different nuclei in a ground state, the R_2 parameter was calculated for each case, the results showed a consistent average square radius of approximately 2.66 femtometers in both the DRMF and RMF frameworks. This value is in line with the 2.71 femtometer value reported in previous studies.

The study examines the potential of recent advancements in parallel-accurate simulation techniques using supervised learning to rapidly and accurately model fluid dynamics at a regional scale, with a focus on the shallow water equations. These equations serve as a fundamental building block in atmospheric circulation and weather prediction systems. While traditional numerical methods are effective for large-scale simulations, they are limited by high computational costs and inaccuracies when simulating complex geometries. The researchers demonstrate that an optimized neural network architecture can learn to predict flow characteristics, including boundary conditions, with remarkable speed and precision in a regional simulation. The model was successfully applied to a simulation of the English Channel, where the O-NET architecture achieved a 10^5 times speedup over a high-order, conservative, and robust numerical method, with minimal accuracy loss. The study suggests that machine learning techniques can enable rapid and precise simulations of complex geophysical fluid dynamics, with potential applications in weather forecasting and other weather-dependent fields.

High dynamic range photography necessitates capturing a scene's variations in brightness by taking multiple exposures and combining them. Determining the optimal exposure settings for combining such photographs is typically done by analyzing the histogram of each image, but this approach fails when some textures are inconspicuous due to low light conditions. Our proposed algorithm automatically decides on the ideal exposure difference and combines images regardless of lighting conditions, by learning from data and utilizing a short sequence of exposure settings to achieve this efficiently on mobile devices.

Causal representation learning through causal graphs has gained significant interest in the AI community due to its robust applications in areas like artificial general intelligence, reliable machine reasoning, and dependable machine learning. However, most current methods for learning such representations rely on complex, non-linear techniques that make them difficult to interpret and hinder further analysis of the underlying simple and causal relationships. This difficulty stems from the inherent challenge in unmixing entangled data without prior knowledge of the underlying structure. In contrast, we investigate whether simple, causal connections can be more effectively captured by leveraging pre-specified structural knowledge. To this end, we develop a novel, flexible neural network framework called Causal Navigators, which allows for end-to-end navigation and inference along a pre-defined causal structure. We demonstrate the framework's versatility by applying it to diverse datasets, including real-world data such as MNHN invertebrates, and achieving state-of-the-art results in both representation learning and goodind inference tasks.

Understanding how heat moves through the layers of catalytic cracking reactors is crucial for optimizing their performance. To better understand this complex process, researchers used a high-speed MRI technique to visualize and measure heat distribution in a stationary bed of spherical particles. By combining the MRI data with computational fluid dynamics simulations, researchers were able to identify three distinct regions of heat distribution: a central area with random heat distribution, an intermediate area with linear heat distribution, and surface layers with quadratic heat distribution. The width of the intermediate area increases with heat difference, and it accounts for a significant portion of the bed when there is a significant temperature difference between the surface and the gas.

In 1976, D Mumford hypothesized that the $b_1$-principle was fundamentally important to understanding complex algebraic surfaces, yet its proof required a deep result by G Ellington in 2015. To date, no comparable argument exists for higher-dimensional objects in higher dimensions and numbers. This work presents a variant of the $b_1$-principle that applies to objects of dimension $n \geq 3$ and numbers of dimension $2$, based on categorical methods involving Descent Data. This research also highlights the potential of applying these modern techniques to address a long-standing problem regarding the rationality of certain varieties, specifically the Fano variety of lines on a cubic threefold.

This study focuses on the intricate nature of cardiac mechanics simulations, which are vital for in-depth heart analysis but demand for efficient computational methods. The research highlights the critical role of multilevel conditioning in solving these complex problems, particularly when using non-linear solvers. To achieve this, the study conducts a comprehensive examination of various multilevel conditioning techniques, taking into account practical factors such as mesh size and computational mesh connectivity. The results indicate that a specific type of multilevel conditioning method offers the most effective balance between computational efficiency and accuracy, with significant potential for further improvement through advanced formulations.

Let $m$ and $k$ be positive integers, and consider an array of i.i.d. random variables $\xi_{m,j}$ indexed from $1$ to $m$ and $1$ to $k$. This indexing can be visualized as a grid of $m$ rows and $k$ columns. Define a random variable $X_{m,k}$ as the maximum sum obtained by dividing the array into $3$ non-overlapping regions using $2$ non-intersecting vertical or horizontal lines. It has been established that when $m$ and $k$ increase at the same rate, the standardized $X_{m,k}$ follows an approximate standard normal distribution. In contrast, it has been shown that when $m$ and $k$ vary significantly, the standardized $X_{m,k}$ converges to the Beta $(2,1)$ distribution. Further research has been conducted to understand the asymptotic behavior of $X_{m,k}$ and a related sequence of random variables $C_{m,k}$, which represents the sum of deviations of $2$ column or row sums from the expected value, which has been estimated including a rate of convergence.

The rapid explosion of user-generated videos on social media platforms has
presented both significant challenges and opportunities for website operators,
with limited options for effectively promoting their sites aside from paid
ads. The emergence of AI video generation technology has addressed several
challenges associated with video creation, prompting several researchers to
explore the potential of developing conversational video generators aimed at
producing highly persuasive and engaging content. Unfortunately, very few existing
surveys comprehensively cover the state-of-the-art techniques in AI-driven
convincing video creation, leaving a significant gap in the field. This work
attempts to address this gap by providing a detailed examination of AI systems
that create both convincing images and videos, with an emphasis on AI-driven
storyboard generation, AI-character animation and AI voice synthesis. The survey
also explores key issues and future research directions in this emerging field.

The words "sense of safety" (SOS) in our society's conversations often fail to accurately reflect the reality, as the term's ambiguity makes it difficult to evaluate, which is also exacerbated by the manipulative language used in marketing and public discourse. This obfuscation makes the true meaning of SOS challenging to evaluate, as evidenced by the inconsistency between the data and the perceived reality. This unexamined reality leads to a false sense of security in our society's discussions. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive definition of the term SOS, offering a measurable metric to assess our society's safety, as well as a method to analyze the effectiveness of various measures in enhancing our society's sense of security.

Recent research has revealed exciting possibilities for combining acoustic and electromagnetic phenomena through mechano-electric coupling in microacoustic metagratings, enabling them to respond effectively even to extremely high-frequency sound, despite their minute size. Regrettably, this breakthrough technology has so far been limited to sound in the ultrasonic range due to the requirement of resonating structures on the order of micrometers. This study presents a significant advancement by resonating a silicon microacoustic metagrating using two-photon lithography, constructing it from nanometric components as small as 100 nanometers. Constructed from atomic layers of piezoelectric silicon, this device can transform ultralow-frequency, microacoustic waves into sound, demonstrating the capability to detect and convert these phenomena even at the **~10^4** level.

In the context of advection-diffusion processes, tracking the mean squared displacement is less useful than tracking the probability distribution function (PDF) due to the often heavy-tailed spatial displacements that occur. While the PDF evolution can be effectively modeled using Laplace transforms, the scenario of randomly distributed obstacles in one-dimensional space has received considerable attention. Such a scenario, where the obstacles are spread out according to an exponential distribution, has been shown to result in anomalous diffusion with a distinct PDF evolution that can be modeled using a combination of modified Bessel functions. In this study, we investigate the impact of different random scenario distributions on the diffusion process, finding that heavy-tailed distributions lead to early-time power-law displacements and Gaussian diffusion at later times, whereas scenario distributions that are stochastically larger than the log-normal distribution exhibit Gaussian diffusion from the earliest times. Furthermore, we derive a generalized equation for the displacement evolution and a rescaling law that can be used to normalize the PDF for a wide range of scenario distributions.

The integration of linear and Kerr nonlinearities is crucial for creating versatile optical systems that go beyond initial experiments. We have formulated a comprehensive, linearly scalable theory that applies to waveguides and optical resonators, capable of accounting for various linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions. This theory utilizes paraxial and slowly varying envelope approximations in conjunction with the Maxwell-Bloch equations, ultimately expressing the system in terms of a single complex amplitude and the Hamiltonian for a waveguide or resonator. By employing this universal approach, researchers can investigate a wide range of linear and Kerr nonlinear phenomena and their interactions, facilitating the design of optically switchable devices with Kerr-induced cross-phase modulation.

This paper builds on Lyapunov-based stability analysis to establish conditions for state-space reachable sets in dynamic systems using unbounded controls.
We will show that certain reachability problems can be solved by finding unbounded control policies that optimize a cost function, and for which the system's trajectory remains stable.
We further prove that optimal state reachable sets can be determined through dynamic programming, and that optimal bounds can be reached with piecewise continuous controls.
To facilitate these results, we introduce a modified Lyapunov stability theorem suitable for unbounded controls and provide examples of its application.
These stability findings are based on generalizations of conversational Lyapunov theorems, a subset of conversational optimization principles.

This study demonstrates the capability of a machine learning model, Generative
Adversarial Networks, in recovering high-resolution details from blurred images of
turbulent fluid flows under specific conditions.  A trained model successfully
reconstructed the intricate structure of a double vortex at different Reynolds
numbers from 100 to 1600, matching observations even when the flow was imaged with
lower-resolution cameras.  At a Reynolds number of 1600, the model achieved a
significant improvement in prediction accuracy with a super-resolution factor of
2.5 when given training data with the same level of blurring as the testing data.  A
control simulation showed that this reduction in camera resolution was equivalent to
a Reynolds number decrease of 1.8 times, thereby revealing the potential for these
models to enhance the study of turbulent flows by accurately reconstructing fine,
elongated structures in these types of flows.

This report discusses the potential of wave function collapse in the solutions to the wave equation, a phenomenon that could have significant implications for the interpretation of interference patterns and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Although this potential issue was initially identified in the context of quantum mechanics, it applies more broadly to wave phenomena and can affect measurements outside of microscopic systems. The report's focus is on a particular experiment involving acoustic waves and initially outlines the necessary equations for the wave equation, adopting standard conventions used in mathematical literature. The example provided and the associated difficulties are thoroughly examined. The wave equation's characteristics for both mathematical and physical quantities are analyzed, revealing the nature of its general solution. The report's findings indicate that energy localization in the form of a wave function collapse is not possible due to the conservative energy conservation law. The implications of this outcome are discussed, along with the consequences for the identified acoustic interference patterns. The report's data suggest that a distinct distinction exists between the mathematical and physical descriptions of the wave equation's one-dimensional plane wave solutions, a phenomenon that could have significant consequences for the interpretation of its mathematical and physical characteristics. The report's outcomes also indicate that a particular observed interference pattern may be explained by the existence of a mathematical, non-physical wave function that arises from the boundary conditions, a phenomenon that could have broader implications for the interpretation of the wave equation's solutions. The report's findings further suggest that a more detailed discussion of the wave function's collapse in the context of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle

Machine learning systems' reliability can be compromised by dynamic environmental changes that the primary model cannot anticipate, leading to model misconfidence.

This issue arises frequently and affects various fields, including medical diagnosis and self-driving technology.

To address this challenge of modeling environmental variability and model guarantee, we introduce an energy-driven open-world uncertainty framework, where closed and open-world uncertainties are separately managed by distinct but complementary loss functions.

Our proposed method allows for a machine's performance to be explicitly tested in response to environmental assurance, enabling real-time systems to reallocate processing resources to meet real-world needs.

To demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, we present the guarantee calibration system, which adjusts the main model's confidence to match actual accuracy, thereby providing real-time machines with real-time confidence.

The results show that our guarantee calibration system achieves precise performance predictions and effective startable guarantees that can be traded for processing resources to meet external assurance needs.

The complete code and models are available on the GitHub repository (https://github.com/huanghaotian/dds).

Despite the success of self-driving technology in certain areas, the notion of creating a robust, adaptable system that can adapt to new, unfamiliar situations remains a significant challenge. This is analogous to the difference between navigating a well-known town and driving in an entirely new town. To address this, the concept of continuous or lifelong learning has been developed, which involves a system acquiring knowledge and adapting to various environments in a continuous, ever-evolving process. A groundbreaking advancement in this field has been achieved through a method that integrates transfer learning and lifelong neural networks into a single, cohesive algorithm. However, testing and evaluating this algorithm has historically been a complex and challenging task. A novel solution to this problem has been introduced with the development of L2Explorer, a pioneering evaluation environment that allows a learning agent to navigate and adapt to various mazes over time.

One of the key challenges in modeling complex systems lies in identifying and managing their underlying patterns. A significant area of focus has been on formalizing processes of specification using declarative methods, particularly through temporal logic and related approaches. This study presents a novel framework built on probabilistic temporal models, offering an integrated system for monitoring and exploring intricate processes in probabilistic temporal settings. The framework, known as P-DAP, leverages techniques from optimal control theory to guide processes towards desired outcomes, offering a comprehensive solution for monitoring and exploring complex processes in probabilistic temporal settings.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, we've observed a unique phenomenon where type II modes transition to type I modes and back again as the system size increases, indicating a partial loss of quasimodularity with measurable consequences. Part of this transition can be attributed to a subset of modes that exhibit increasing bandwidth with system expansion, effectively decoupling from the global structure and showing varying periods related to short-order approximants. The exclusion of this subset reveals a distinct increase in mode density within specific sequences of quasicrystalline structures, and this work presents potential optical platforms for studying this intricate behavior of modes in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals.

Liger, the High-Resolution Near-Infrared System on the Keck II Telescope, is now operational and has already collected science data. This document provides an overview of the development of the data processing system for Liger, along with the associated software tools. Furthermore, it discusses the integration of the software to stream and display data in real-time, the the characteristics of the observation modes, the development of the software to manage the instrument, the calibration procedures, the data processing workflow, the software used to monitor the instrument, the distribution of the software, and the integration with the observatory's system.

We propose a method to enhance the resolution of identifying the spatial mode distribution of a single-photon beam using bi-photon correlations between two photons that have passed through separate optical systems. By measuring the correlation in a specific mode, such as a Hermite-Gauss distribution, we find that the effective resolution is significantly improved, exceeding the diffraction limit associated with resolving single-photon images. The super-resolution effect is directly related to the ratio of the actual aperture size to the sample size, and we demonstrate a theoretical increase in resolution of up to $\sqrt{2}$ when aperture sizes are set at one focal length and sample sizes at half that distance. This demonstrates the potential for bi-photon correlations to achieve remarkable improvements in resolution through the separation of photons in a specific way.
This note provides an overview of various approaches to compactifying moduli spaces, using specific examples, and discusses the interconnections between the different methods.

In the context of land management and conservation efforts, understanding the short-term fluctuations in ecosystem data is of significant importance. This examination applies to a wide array of monitoring datasets, including those tracking the population of large animals in North American ecosystems, often referred to as the trophic mosaic. While the topic has been extensively analyzed using mathematical models, the case studies available are limited and primarily focused on the whooping crane population. This paper is intended to address this gap by providing the framework for incorporating large animal population data into a North American whooping crane management plan. The underlying statistical methodology outlined here will offer the basis for identifying potential indicators of population changes in the whooping crane plan. This framework is specifically designed to account for the effects of natural environmental fluctuations and can be applied to any large animal dataset within the ecosystem. The proposed statistical examination utilizes a novel approach known as the local regression with respect to a sliding time window. This allows for the identification of short-term fluctuations in animal populations, often referred to as the fast and slow timescales. The magnitude of fluctuations on the fast timescale is measured using a local coefficient of variation, while the energy of fluctuations on the two timescales is measured using a localized Hilbert transform. The results obtained from this examination are presented in a user-friendly format, including visual scatter plots and color-coded heat maps. These tools can be easily integrated into standard ecosystem monitoring and management practices.

When comparing star formation rates to the Mendieta-Schmidt relation, a distinct correlation becomes apparent across the major sequences of the UMF.
New analyses using WISE and K-band data for 2362 local galaxies with reliable measurements in the literature are employed to investigate the role of bulge properties in this relationship's connection sequence.
A significant correlation is found between star formation rates and V-band bulge luminosity, supporting hypotheses suggesting that quenching within central bulges drives the observed rates.
Further analysis reveals a stronger correlation exists when separating galaxies by bulge-to-total (B/T) ratio, particularly for those with B/T greater than 0.3, as seen in a color-color plot where red galaxies populate the upper half.
A hypothesis proposes that quenching in significant bulges typically occurs within galaxies already naturally redder due to those bulges themselves.

This study traverses linguistic barriers in sentiment assessment by adapting
state-of-the-art Arabic models for use in Turkish. As annotated Arabic data is
unavailable for direct adaptation, the authors employ a text-to-text translation
methodology. English texts corresponding to Arabic sources are obtained via
Google Translate, and Arabic texts are generated from these English versions using
Google's reverse translation service. The resulting synthetic datasets are used to
train The Model, which is also compared to The Baseline Model trained on translated
English data. The results indicate that The Model outperforms the Baseline Model
on real Turkish data, surpassing random chance accuracy by 10%. Furthermore, The
Model exhibits robustness, achieving comparable performance to the Baseline Model
with only 10% lower accuracy when evaluated on Arabic and English sentiment data.

The effectiveness of Barriers in preventing information dissemination within networks is well-documented Barriers force target individuals to undergo a cognitive process, which research suggests can be受限于 Barriers with the Mending Protocol, the evaluation process is shortened, rendering Barriers less effective. However, there's concern that individuals may recognize the Mending Protocol's impact and place less value on the evaluation process, thus strengthening Barriers. This research proposes that Barriers in electronic messaging systems can be effectively lengthened to hinder the flow of information. The study aims to evaluate the Mendable Protocol's benefits and drawbacks with the Mending Barriers Experiment. The results show that Barriers implemented in the Mending Protocol lead to heightened activation of the prefrontal cortex among participants, contributing to the conclusion that Barriers in the Mending Protocol serve as effective tools for limiting the dissemination of information among individuals in computer networks.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if a finite subset S of an abelian group G has a small number of sums (2k-3 <= k^2), then subset S can be mapped onto a subset A of an integer group Z with a small size difference (|S| >= |A| - 1) based on a limited k value (2 <= k <= k_0). 

We've achieved a breakthrough in this theory's integer group variant by enhancing the lower bound of k to 65, thus achieving k >= 65. 

This advancement signifies the first instance of increasing the lower bound of k in the context of this theoretical framework.

We analyze the set of paths of fractional Brownian motion (with Hurwitz parameter $H$ between 0 and 1) in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that can be represented as the sum of a fixed deterministic drift at time one and a small-scaled independent fractional Brownian motion (with the same Hurwitz parameter $H$). We prove that this set has a positive Lebesgue measure and an interior that is also non-empty, with respect to the standard $d$-dimensional measure, for all paths of the given fractional Brownian motion, where the determination of this Hurwitz parameter does not depend on the dimension of the space in which this set resides.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we derive a simplified form of the H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian that accounts for quantum effects, following a specific transformation. Consequently, the Hamiltonian's structure is modified, and the original classical H\'enon-Heiles dynamics are disrupted. Through numerical simulation, it is shown that the modified Hamiltonian displays only regular behavior in contrast to the H\'enon-Heiles system that exhibits both regular and chaotic behavior.

The timely allocation of limited intensive care units (ICUs) is crucial for maximizing patient survival rates, underscoring the need to predict ICU admissions as early as possible. ICU patients experience higher mortality rates than those who do not require intensive care, and timely identification of high-risk patients is essential for effective resource allocation. Although clinical indicators can help predict ICU use, radiological features, including X-ray and CT scans, contain vital information about high-risk patients that is not fully understood. This study aims to explore the potential for identifying ICU admission predictors from low-dose CT data, a common imaging method for COVID-19 diagnosis. By leveraging both clinical information and radiological features extracted from X-ray and CT scans, machine learning models were trained to predict ICU admissions. The results showed that combining clinical indicators and low-dose CT features led to the highest accuracy. Notably, radiological features alone performed comparably to clinical indicators in terms of prediction accuracy. This research highlights the value of medical images in forecasting ICU admissions and sets the stage for further investigation into using advanced imaging data to predict patient outcomes.

A functor $G\colon \mathcal{E}\to \mathcal{B}$ between simplicial categories is considered a simplicial bundle if it maps simplicial limits to simplicial limits and we show that such functors preserve and reflect group simplicial structures. It is demonstrated that representable functors are group simplicial and thus preserve this structure when composed. We also prove that all $\mathcal{E}$-group simplicial bundles have associated group simplicial total objects. The key to our approach lies in establishing that all such bundles have accessible local right adjoints, which ultimately allow us to reflect group simplicial total objects.

Despite significant progress in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), current models struggle to accurately identify difficult relationships, especially when the objects involved are unrelated. This issue results in a high number of false positives, which in turn, hampers the models' performance. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive dataset called Conquer-VRD, which contains 10,000 challenging relationships between common COCO objects. This dataset serves as an ideal benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of VRD models. Building on this dataset, we devised two approaches to enhance the models' ability to recognize difficult relationships. The first approach, which we call Easy-VRND, focuses on localizing the negative object using the relationship phrase. The second approach, which we call Hard-VRND, does so by leveraging both the relationship phrase and the pre-detected easy object. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed methods result in substantial reductions in false positives for challenging relationships, while having a minimal impact on other relationships.

A state-of-the-art activity recognition framework based on deep learning requires a significant amount of labeled training data. In scenarios where extensive data labeling is impractical, our proposed method, Delta Sampling R-BERT (DSRB), achieves accurate activity classification with very limited labeled information. DSRB initially employs a deep learning architecture to identify potential activities from various possibilities, then focuses on sampling uncertain data points for labeling. This process is repeated in an iterative manner to enhance classification performance. DSRB effectively ranks data points by uncertainty during each sampling iteration and is capable of identifying hidden, low-light activities. Experimental results show that DSRA significantly boosts accuracy compared to other methods, requiring only a fraction of the data that the baseline approach relies on.

Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) have been utilized in both special purpose computing and prototyping due to their customizable nature. While previous designs focused on data parallelism with 1D or 2D arrays, they fell short in exploiting spatial and temporal reconfigurability of FPGAs. A novel concurrent processing unit called Data Addressable FPGA (DA-FGA) was developed to utilize all available resources, utilizing a non-contiguous memory address for each processing element. The DA-FGA employs independent pixelated and bitmap units for the PE and utilizes a decoupled architecture to enhance its performance. By integrating these features, the DA-FGA can utilize a larger number of processing elements, resulting in significant improvements in throughput and latency when compared to traditional units.

At a redshift of 3 in a galaxy galaxy cluster, a massive, left-leaning disk galaxy is found that emits both X-ray and optical light. This galaxy exhibits an unusual bulge-disk ratio, typically associated with slow-rotating $S0$ galaxies, yet it exhibits a significant left-leaning bulge, and the galaxy itself is accreting a massive gas tail from the cluster. By analyzing the galaxy's properties, researchers have determined that it has a massive, left-leaning disk that spans approximately 25 kiloparsecs and exhibits significant star formation in its inner regions. This galaxy appears to be in an early stage of assembly, with its disk skewed to one side, and it accounts for a significant portion of the galaxy cluster's mass. By comparing this observation to simulations, researchers have determined that tidal forces may have contributed to the galaxy's bulge formation and that it is expected to transform into an extremely massive, bulge-dominant galaxy by a redshift of 1.5.

Researchers have long debated whether the observed pattern of flavour in the Standard Model is a coincidence or a necessary aspect of the theory, given its complexity. One aspect of this investigation involves flavour's global structure, which remains unclear due to the vast parameter space. In this study, we employ a set of 1000 simulated universives to examine this issue, allowing us to identify any 'structure zeros' – universives where certain flavour patterns are impossible. Our analysis reveals that these anomalies are typically isolated incidents and that, in many cases, they can be attributed to second-order effects. A key limitation of this study is its reliance on a simulated environment, which prevents a comprehensive examination of low-dimensional structure zeros. In this instance, we found that a particular pair of fermions sharing the same mass scale is feasible, albeit with a narrow margin. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings for the real universe, considering various theories that attempt to address the mystery of flavour's origin.

This study investigates the "bubbling" solutions of a critical nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, specifically -Delta u - 1/(|x|^{beta}) u + Q(x) u = u^{(N+2)/(N-2)} for u in H^{1}_{loc}(R^N). We establish conditions under which no bubbling solutions exist. We also examine the behavior near the origin, focusing on how solutions can be translated while maintaining a sequence of bubbling solutions. Finally, we establish a connection between the index of a bubbling solution and its periodicity, establishing a lower bound of N-2 for the periodicity. This bound becomes N-2 under the condition that Q(x) exhibits Q(e^{(2pi/omega) x}) is periodic with a period omega in directions transverse to the origin.

Recent advances in deep learning, particularly in character-level sequence prediction models, have reached human-parity performance on various English text tasks. Despite this, the same models fall short when it comes to programming languages, consistently yielding code with significant bug rates. Current techniques for enhancing synthesized code quality are primarily limited to statistical metrics and manual validation. In this study, we introduce a novel approach that integrates static analysis into the feedback loop for characterization analysis during the generation process. This approach leverages the capabilities of static analysis to supplement the feedback provided by 1-to-1 token prediction models during code generation. As a result, our integrated system produces code that is 14% less buggy than the code produced using only characterization analysis, 17% less buggy than the code produced using only static analysis, 12% less buggy after applying CodeLlama 7B as the prediction model, and 25% less buggy after applying GPT-J 6B as the prediction baseline on three widely-used code synthesis benchmarks.

On the 7th of November in 2004, a powerful solar event took place at position 095, with a peak intensity of 2.0 x 10-3 W/m2 at 255 Å, hitting the Earth between 05:12 and 05:22 UT. This event was accompanied by a significant outburst in X-rays and protons that exceeded the threshold of 20 MeV, and there were also indications of neutrons in data from ground-based water Cherenkov detectors in Hida and Mizusawa in Japan, as well as the Kanazawa Muon Telescope Project. Analysis of the rate of photons detected in Mizusawa revealed a connection between the effects of protons and neutrons, and the peak neutron signal was delayed by about 12 minutes relative to the peak proton signal. By assuming that secondary pions decay into both photons and neutrons in equal measure, and accounting for energy losses of neutrons as they travel to the surface of the Earth, the energy spectrum of solar protons was found to be consistent with a peak around 20 GeV, and the presence of neutrons was attributed to the presence of secondary neutrons and nucleons created by cosmic ray interactions in the Earth's atmosphere.
